bp: Online conversation uses emojis as small public signs of identity, mood, and belonging. Skin-tone modifiers matter because a person can choose a symbol that looks closer to them instead of accepting one supposedly neutral default. The problem begins when web platforms ask language systems to read, rank, summarize, moderate, or generate text that contains these symbols. If the system treats the same hand gesture differently when the skin tone changes, it can quietly attach unequal meaning or feeling to people who are trying to express the same action. This paper studies that risk directly. It compares two kinds of models: dedicated emoji representation models, built specifically to turn emojis into machine-readable descriptions, and modern large language models, built for broader language tasks. The real question is not whether a model can display a colored emoji. It is whether the model's internal treatment keeps meaning stable across skin tones or imports social bias into a basic communication tool.
wh: The difficulty is that the harm is subtle. A skin-toned emoji is not a long sentence with an explicit stereotype that can be flagged by a rule. It is a symbol whose meaning should mostly come from the base emoji, such as the gesture or face, while the tone modifier should preserve personal identity. A system can appear to support the symbol technically while still assigning different neighborhoods of meaning to different tones. The abstract says the study looks at semantic consistency, representational similarity, sentiment polarity, and core biases because no single test is enough. Similarity can reveal whether two versions of the same emoji are placed near each other. Sentiment can reveal whether one tone is treated as more positive or negative. Bias probes can reveal repeated unequal associations. The challenge is also comparative: older specialized emoji models and general language models may fail in different ways, so a serious audit must separate lack of support from deeper unequal meaning.
naive: A smart beginner might assume that skin tone is just a harmless visual add-on. The obvious solution would be to strip the modifier away, treat every thumbs-up or waving hand as the same base emoji, and let the model handle the rest. That fails because the modifier is part of identity and inclusion; removing it erases the user's chosen expression. Another beginner move would be to check only whether the model recognizes the symbol at all. That also fails. Recognition says the model can process the character, not that it gives comparable meaning to different tones. A model could understand every modifier and still attach lower sentiment, weaker similarity, or inconsistent associations to some of them.
ap: The paper's central move is to turn skin-tone treatment into a set of measurable comparisons. Instead of asking whether a model supports emojis in the abstract, it asks what changes when the same emoji is shown with different skin tones. The authors compare dedicated emoji models, emoji2vec and emoji-sw2v, with four large language models: Llama, Gemma, Qwen, and Mistral. For each model class, they inspect whether skin-tone variants remain meaningfully close, whether their meanings stay consistent, whether their emotional scores tilt in unequal directions, and whether broader bias tests expose systematic disparities. This is an audit rather than a new chat feature. The point is to make hidden representational harm visible: if the only intended difference is skin tone, then large changes in meaning or sentiment become evidence that the model is carrying more social information than the user asked it to carry.
mech: The mechanism starts with a controlled object: an emoji that can appear with skin-tone modifiers. The input to the audit is not just one symbol, but a family of related symbols where the base action or expression is held steady while the tone changes. Each tested model turns those symbols into an internal machine-readable representation or produces behavior that can be compared across variants. For dedicated emoji models, the comparison likely centers on the stored numeric descriptions they assign to emojis. For language models, the study can examine how well they support the modifiers and how their outputs or internal representations treat them. The paper then asks several linked questions. First, support: does the model meaningfully handle the skin-tone version rather than breaking or collapsing it? Second, semantic consistency: does a darker-toned waving hand still carry the same core meaning as a lighter-toned waving hand? Third, representational similarity: are variants of the same base emoji placed near each other by the model's comparison machinery? Fourth, sentiment polarity: does the emotional direction become more positive or negative depending on tone? Fifth, core bias: do repeated association tests show disparities that cannot be explained by the base emoji alone? The output is a comparative bias map across model classes, showing both severe deficiencies in specialized emoji models and systemic disparities in meaning and sentiment.
math: The main mathematical idea is similarity: turning a rich symbol into a compact description and then asking how near two descriptions are. In plain terms, the model builds a map where emojis that mean similar things should sit close together. If two versions of the same gesture differ only by skin tone, they should usually stay close on that map. A large gap means the model is treating the tone as if it changes the meaning more than it should. The second idea is consistency under controlled change. One part of the input changes, the tone modifier, while the base symbol stays fixed; the audit measures whether the output changes only in ways that are justified. The third idea is sentiment scoring, which turns emotional leaning into a comparable quantity: more positive, more negative, or somewhere between. This is useful because bias can appear as a small repeated tilt rather than an obvious wrong label. The fourth idea is group comparison under fairness pressure. The groups are not people in a dataset but skin-tone variants of communication symbols. The tradeoff is representation versus erasure: the system must preserve the user's chosen identity marker while not allowing that marker to trigger unequal meaning. The math fits because the harm is relational. It lives in differences between versions that should be treated comparably.
dots: This paper sits in the repo's fairness and bias family because it asks how automated systems reuse past patterns without turning social imbalance into neutral-looking evidence. It connects especially to the recurring conference idea of similarity: many systems place words, images, users, or symbols on a learned map and then make decisions from nearness. Here, the map itself is under audit. If skin-tone variants are not near their base meaning, downstream search, moderation, recommendation, or generation can inherit that error. It also connects to the information concept in the current data: a change is informative when it changes what the system believes. In this paper, the dangerous case is that skin tone changes too much, revealing hidden bias instead of useful meaning. Neighboring fairness papers study biased rankings, graph links, retrieval answers, cultural moderation, and vision shortcuts. This work is the emoji version of the same deeper problem: a visible identity signal enters a model, and the system must prove it did not turn that signal into unequal treatment.
ww: The audit works because it uses controlled comparison rather than vague judgment. If two inputs differ in many ways, it is hard to know why a model behaves differently. Skin-toned emoji variants give a cleaner test: hold the base symbol steady and change the tone. That makes unequal shifts easier to interpret. Looking across several measures also matters. A model could pass a basic support check while failing sentiment consistency. It could keep variants fairly close in one comparison but still show biased associations in another. By studying dedicated emoji models and large language models side by side, the paper avoids assuming that specialization means fairness or that general language ability means emoji competence. The reported performance gap is important for exactly that reason: a tool built for emojis can still be deficient if it was trained before skin-tone modifiers were well represented or if its comparison space compresses them poorly. The broader bias findings become more credible because they are not tied to one model or one metric. Repeated disparities across semantic consistency, similarity, sentiment, and association tests point to a structural problem in representation, not a one-off display bug.
po: The payoff is an audit lens for a real web communication problem. The paper shows that large language models have stronger support for skin-tone modifiers than widely used specialized emoji models, while also showing that support is not the same as fairness. Its multi-part investigation finds skewed sentiment and inconsistent meanings across skin tones, which gives platform developers concrete reasons to test these symbols before using model outputs in moderation, search, recommendation, or generated replies. The practical gain is not a finished debiasing method. It is evidence that emoji representation harms can be measured at scale and should be part of responsible model evaluation.
limits: The abstract supports conclusions about model representations and comparative disparities, but it does not prove how often these biases harm users in live products. The study depends on the chosen emoji set, bias tests, sentiment measures, and model versions. Similarity and sentiment scores are useful warning signs, but they do not capture every cultural meaning of an emoji or every conversational context. The paper also audits existing models rather than showing that a mitigation removes the problem. For the findings to guide deployment, platforms must connect these representation tests to actual downstream uses and repeat them as models, emoji standards, and online language change.
